design_detail: Population birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study; 1265 children born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977). Self-reported use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants for the period since the previous interview, and self-reported psychotic symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25 and since the previous assessment at 30 and 35, both reported at the interviews at ages 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (use periods 16–18 to 30–35); population-averaged logistic and negative binomial generalized estimating equations, unadjusted and adjusted for fixed childhood, family and adolescent confounders and for time-varying covariates; dose-response by lifetime highest frequency of use; comparison of symptoms at 30–35 by past and current use. Read: all pages of the online-first PDF (pp. 1–8, pages numbered as printed on that version; print pages 987–994); Figure 1 is an image whose values were not extracted; Supplementary Tables S1 to S3 not read.
can_establish: Whether, in a general-population cohort, periods of methamphetamine use go with more self-reported psychotic symptoms at the same interview after adjustment for measured childhood, family, adolescent and time-varying factors, and whether that excess is concentrated in frequent use.
cannot_establish: Which came first (use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, and at ages 18, 21 and 25 over different windows: use since the previous interview, symptoms over the past month); effects on clinical psychotic disorder (the outcome is self-reported symptom items with high base rates); effects of very frequent use (few participants used often); and whether the findings hold outside one city's 1977 birth cohort.

sample.recruitment: Birth cohort of 1265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977, studied at birth, at 4 months, yearly to age 16 and at 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort members with at least one completed wave of data at ages 18 to 35 (p. 3).
sample.demographics: 635 male and 630 female at birth; the analysed samples (79–82% of the surviving cohort at each age) under-represented people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds (low parental education, low socioeconomic status, single parenthood) (pp. 3–4).
sample.attrition: 18–21% of the surviving cohort missing at each wave; the GEE models used everyone with at least one wave, and weighting for the pattern of missing data gave essentially the same results (p. 4); the authors note that people with psychotic symptoms, particularly paranoid ideas, are less likely to be retained (p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: Little selection into the study (a birth cohort); selective loss of disadvantaged participants, and possibly of people with paranoid symptoms, could bias estimates toward the null if those groups also used methamphetamine more; frequent use is rare (51 people ever used at least weekly).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each interview of any use of 'methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc' since the previous interview, and how often; amphetamine-type stimulants were not distinguished, but the authors state that methamphetamine was by far the most common in New Zealand over the period (p. 2). Use or no use in each period for the repeated-measures models; lifetime highest frequency (never, once or twice, up to about monthly, at least weekly) for the dose-response model.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Use in the period: 3.3% (ages 16–18), 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30), 7.8% (30–35); ever 28.8% (Table 1, p. 4). Highest frequency: once or twice 124 (11.9%), up to about monthly 117 (11.3%), at least weekly 51 (4.9%) (Table 3, p. 7). Amount and route not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Frequency of cannabis use and alcohol use disorder were time-varying covariates in the fully adjusted model; other illicit drug use was not adjusted for, beyond adolescent affiliation with substance-using peers (pp. 2–3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews (symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, and since the previous assessment at 30 and 35).

comparison.controls: Within the cohort: periods with and without reported use (population-averaged estimates), and people by lifetime highest frequency against those who never used.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment. Fixed confounders: family living standards; family instability; parental intimate-partner violence; parental alcohol problems, criminality and illicit drug use; parental bonding; childhood sexual abuse and physical punishment; sex; childhood conduct and attention problems; adolescent self-esteem, novelty seeking, conduct disorder, anxiety disorder and affiliation with delinquent or substance-using peers. Time-varying covariates: major depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol use disorder, frequency of cannabis use and life stress (pp. 2–3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis and earlier psychotic experiences are not among the listed covariates, and genetic liability is unmeasured; the E-value indicates that an unmeasured confounder associated with both exposure and outcome by an odds ratio of about 1.6 could explain the fully adjusted association (p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Periods without methamphetamine use include use of other drugs; cannabis and alcohol are adjusted for, other drugs are not.

outcomes.instruments: Psychotic symptom items from the Symptom Checklist 90 (ages 18, 21 and 25; past month) and from the Diagnostic Interview Schedule (ages 30 and 35; since the previous assessment), covering hallucinations, delusions, paranoid ideation and related symptoms; the items are in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2, not read (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Coefficient alpha 0.71 to 0.75; an earlier factor analysis found the SCL-90 items formed one scale (p. 2). The authors note that some SCL-90 items (for example feeling lonely with others) arguably do not capture genuine psychotic experiences; 35.2% to 41.8% reported at least one symptom in the periods to age 25 (Table 1; p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: At least one symptom in the period (dichotomous) and number of symptoms (count); not a diagnosis of psychotic disorder (p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two outcome measures at three levels of adjustment, plus a dose-response model, a comparison of past and current use and a sensitivity analysis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; exposure and outcome were both self-reported in the same interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Any use vs none, at least one psychotic symptom: OR 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted; 2.14 (1.70–2.71) adjusted for fixed confounders; 1.33 (1.03–1.72) adjusted also for time-varying covariates (p = 0.033). Number of symptoms: IRR 1.50 (1.26–1.78), 1.52 (1.26–1.85) and 1.24 (1.02–1.50) (p = 0.030) (Table 2, p. 6; p. 4). E-value 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11) (p. 4). Dose-response, adjusted for fixed confounders only: once or twice 1.37 (0.86–2.17), up to about monthly 1.32 (0.82–2.11), at least weekly 2.85 (1.21–6.69; p = 0.016) (Table 3, p. 7). Population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), assuming causality (p. 6). Symptoms at 30–35: 5.1% of those who never used (n = 672), 7.4% of those who used only before 30 (n = 215), 15.9% of those who used before 30 and at 30–35 (n = 69), p = 0.0009 (Table 4, p. 7).
analysis.covariates: Fixed confounders and time-varying covariates as listed under comparison. The dose-response model used only the fixed confounders that were significant predictors in Model 1: family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peer affiliation and attention problems (p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All three levels of adjustment are reported for both outcomes; the dose-response estimate that the abstract reports beside the fully adjusted one comes from a model with a smaller covariate set chosen by statistical significance and no time-varying covariates.
analysis.power: With an effective sample of 1056, at least 90% power to detect odds ratios of 1.2 (p. 3); sparse frequent use prevented repeated-measures dose-response models (p. 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Periods of any methamphetamine use went with modestly higher odds of self-reported psychotic symptoms at the same interview after full adjustment (OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72); the excess was concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (OR 2.85, adjusted for fixed confounders only); people who had used only before age 30 reported symptoms at 30–35 about as often as those who never used (7.4% vs 5.1%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion states that "methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for psychosis in the general population" (p. 7). Gaps: (1) the outcome is self-reported psychotic-like symptoms with high base rates, not psychosis as a disorder; (2) use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews (at ages 18 to 25 over different windows, although the abstract says both covered the period since the previous interview), so the phrase risk factor implies an order the design cannot show; (3) the abstract places the at-least-weekly estimate (2.85) directly after the estimate adjusted for concurrent cannabis use, but the 2.85 is adjusted only for fixed childhood, family and adolescent factors; (4) the discussion's statement that no long-term persistence was found among people with frequent use rests on Table 4, which groups people by any use, not by frequency; (5) the abstract calls the comparison at 30–35 incidence, but Table 4 gives the share reporting symptoms in that period, including people with earlier symptoms. The authors acknowledge the measurement problem and the sparse frequent use (p. 7).

timeline.event: Prospective within-person cohort of people who use methamphetamine showing dose-related psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2013), sharing an author with this study.
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis: frequency of use the factor with the strongest evidence (Arunogiri et al., 2018).
Meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use, mostly from clinical and criminal-justice samples (McKetin et al., 2019); this cohort is not in it (search May 2017).
This study (online 2021, print 2023): the first longitudinal general-population estimate, by the authors' account (p. 6).
Ten-year retrospective cohort of incident psychosis in people with illicit amphetamine records (Huang et al., 2022); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only general-population longitudinal estimate read so far. It agrees in direction with the clinical literature and gives a smaller association after adjustment for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors, concentrated in frequent use. It shares an author (McKetin) with the 2013 cohort and the 2019 meta-analysis but uses an independent sample.

funding.funder: The Christchurch Health and Development Study is funded by the Health Research Council of New Zealand (Programme Grant 16/600) (p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Otago (Christchurch and Wellington) and the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; R. McKetin is also an author of the 2013 within-person cohort and of the 2019 meta-analysis that this paper compares itself with.

what_would_settle_it: A pooled analysis of several general-population cohorts with frequent assessments, clinically validated psychosis outcomes, measured family history of psychosis and other drug use, and enough frequent methamphetamine use to model within-person changes in frequency, so that the timing of use relative to symptom onset and recovery after stopping can be estimated.

domains.note: Rich prospective adjustment for childhood, family and adolescent factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; family history of psychosis and other drug use not adjusted. Adjusting for depression and anxiety, which may follow from use or accompany psychotic symptoms, could bias toward the null. The dose-response estimate (2.85) is adjusted for fixed confounders only and on its own would be at high risk in this domain.
Self-reported use over periods of up to five years, without biological verification; amphetamine-type stimulants not distinguished; coarse frequency categories.
Birth cohort followed from before exposure; losses at follow-up are judged under missing data.
No intervention relevant to the question.
18–21% of the surviving cohort missing at each wave, under-representing disadvantaged participants; weighting gave the same pattern; possible differential loss of people with paranoid symptoms.

Self-reported symptom items reported in the same interview as drug use, and at ages 18, 21 and 25 for the past month while use covered the years since the previous interview, so exposure and outcome windows differ in three of the five waves (the paper says the difference was corrected in the analyses without saying how, p. 2); the instrument changed between ages 25 and 30 (the scale-by-exposure interaction was not significant, p = 0.13); some items of doubtful validity, though removing two of them did not change the results.
No registered analysis plan; the dose-response model uses a covariate set chosen by statistical significance; otherwise every adjustment level and both outcomes are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No domain is at high risk, but concerns in five domains bear on a modest estimate (OR 1.33, lower limit 1.03): unmeasured confounding of the size the E-value describes (about 1.6), same-interview self-report of exposure and outcome and differential attrition could each move it to the null or beyond, which substantially lowers confidence in it as an estimate of the effect of use (ROBINS-E: some concerns in several domains). A second reader may reasonably judge some concerns overall; the study remains the best general-population evidence read so far. It may be cited for the adjusted association with self-reported psychotic symptoms and for its concentration in frequent use, not for causation or for psychotic disorder.

key_findings.finding: Birth cohort of 1265 (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977; 1025, 1011, 1003, 987 and 962 analysed at ages 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (79–82% of the surviving cohort), under-representing socially disadvantaged backgrounds; weighting for missing data gave essentially the same results.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants (p. 2); Sample size and sample bias (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: Use in the period: 3.3% (ages 16–18), 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30), 7.8% (30–35), ever 28.8%; at least one psychotic symptom: 35.2%, 41.8%, 36.4%, 9.9% and 6.4%, ever 66.3%; the drop after age 25 partly reflects the change of instrument.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Rates of methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms over time

key_findings.finding: Any methamphetamine use in a period vs none, odds of reporting at least one psychotic symptom at the same interview: 1.88 (1.55–2.30) unadjusted; 2.14 (1.70–2.71) adjusted for fixed childhood, family and adolescent confounders; 1.33 (1.03–1.72) adjusted also for time-varying major depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol use disorder, frequency of cannabis use and life stress (p = 0.033). Number of symptoms: IRR 1.50 (1.26–1.78), 1.52 (1.26–1.85), 1.24 (1.02–1.50) (p = 0.030).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Time-dynamic covariate factors (p. 3); Results › Associations … before and after control for covariates, numbered points 1 and 2 (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Table 2 calls the fully adjusted model Model 2; the results text calls it Model 3.

key_findings.finding: The E-value for unmeasured confounding was 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11); the scale-by-exposure interaction was not significant (p = 0.13).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations … before and after control for covariates, numbered points 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Lifetime highest frequency (adjusted for fixed confounders only): once or twice 1.37 (0.86–2.17), up to about monthly 1.32 (0.82–2.11), at least weekly 2.85 (1.21–6.69; p = 0.016), against never (747, 71.9%); 51 people (4.9%) had ever used at least weekly.
key_findings.note: The model's covariates are childhood family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peer affiliation and attention problems; child IQ is not among the confounders listed in the methods. The categories are not monotonic (1.37 for once or twice, 1.32 for up to about monthly, 2.85 for at least weekly), so the pattern is a contrast between at least weekly use (51 people) and the rest rather than a gradient.

key_findings.finding: Removing two SCL-90 items of doubtful face validity gave equivalent results; the population attributable fraction was 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), assuming causality.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Population attributable fraction (PAF) estimate (p. 3); Results › Sensitivity analyses; Estimate of the population attributable fraction (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: At ages 30–35, at least one psychotic symptom was reported by 5.1% of those who never used (n = 672), 7.4% of those who used only before age 30 (n = 215) and 15.9% of those who used before 30 and at 30–35 (n = 69; Mantel-Haenszel p = 0.0009); among those with a symptom before 30, 6.3% (415), 8.3% (156) and 21.6% (51) (p = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Proximal/distal use of methamphetamine (p. 6); Table 4 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: Grouped by any use, not by frequency; the text describes the third group as having used both before age 35 and at 30–35. The never against past-only comparison is not tested separately: counts reconstructed from the percentages (34 of 672 and 16 of 215) give a relative risk of about 1.47 (95% CI about 0.83 to 2.6; editors' calculation), so the data do not exclude a moderate lasting excess, and the abstract's finding of no evidence for a persistent vulnerability is an absence of evidence.

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the change of psychosis measure during follow-up, SCL-90 items that may not capture genuine psychotic experiences, a sample born in one place and year, likely lower retention of people with paranoid ideas, and sparse use and symptoms in later periods.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 labels the fully adjusted model Model 2, while the results text calls it Model 3 (numbered point 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling only; the 1.33 and 1.24 estimates come from the model with both fixed and time-varying covariates.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the at-least-weekly odds ratio (2.85) immediately after the estimates adjusted for time-varying factors including concurrent cannabis use, but Table 3 is adjusted for fixed confounders only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency gradient has not been adjusted for concurrent cannabis or alcohol use and should not be cited as if it had.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the comparison at ages 30–35 as incidence of psychotic symptoms, but Table 4 gives the share reporting symptoms in that period, including people with earlier symptoms; the text describes the third group as having used before age 35 rather than before 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: The persistence analysis is a period prevalence by any past use; it does not test persistence after frequent use.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariates of the dose-response model include child IQ, which is not among the confounding factors listed in the methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the dose-response covariate set is not fully described where the confounders are defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that at each interview participants reported their use and their psychotic symptoms for the period since the previous interview, but the Methods give the past month for symptoms at ages 18, 21 and 25 (since the previous assessment only at 30 and 35), and say the difference in time frames was corrected in the analyses without saying how.
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure and outcome windows differ in three of the five waves; a claim should say that use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, not for the same periods.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the window of the highest frequency of use and of the symptom outcome as ages 18–35, while the Methods (p. 3) and the dose–response paragraph (p. 6) call it lifetime, ages 16–35.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling inconsistency; whether use at 16–18 counts in the dose–response categories is unclear.
